strengths: The application of data attribution and influence functions to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) is a conceptually natural and interesting research direction, as understanding the role of specific collocation points and boundary conditions remains a core challenge in scientific machine learning.

The mathematical formulation in the appendix clearly articulates how the standard implicit-function-theorem-based influence function framework extends to stationary points and composite losses, including perturbations to PDE parameters and loss weights.

The paper introduces intuitive domain-specific heuristic indicators (Directional Indicator and Region Indicator) to check whether trained models capture expected physical phenomena (e.g., flow directionality and cylinder influence).
weaknesses: The manuscript is excessively brief and underdeveloped for a full conference paper (the main text spans only 4 pages), leaving critical components unfinished (e.g., missing code URLs in the abstract and Section 'Code Availability').

There is no empirical validation of the accuracy of the influence estimates themselves. Standard influence function literature (e.g., Koh & Liang, 2017) validates approximations against actual retraining (leave-one-out or group retraining). Without verifying that predicted counterfactual changes align with actual retraining under the non-convex PINN loss landscape, it is unclear whether the computed influences are faithful.

The experimental evaluation is very limited, covering only a single 2D steady-state Navier-Stokes benchmark and comparing only three hand-crafted configurations (good, missing convective term, and reduced sample size). A broader set of PDEs (e.g., transient flows, advection-diffusion, or wave equations) and failure modes is needed.

Practical scalability and conditioning are not adequately addressed. Because the PINN loss contains spatial derivatives of the network output, computing and inverting the parameter Hessian $\mathcal{H}$ can be ill-conditioned and expensive. The paper relies on `NaiveInfluenceFunction` for a small 4-layer MLP without discussing Hessian damping, curvature estimation, or scalability to standard-size scientific ML architectures.

The proposed indicators (DI and RI) remain largely descriptive post-hoc diagnostics. The paper does not demonstrate how these insights can be leveraged algorithmically to debug or improve PINN training (e.g., adaptive sampling or loss re-weighting driven by influence values).

strengths: The core idea of applying training data attribution via influence functions to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) is conceptually interesting and well-motivated for model interpretability and debugging.
The appendix provides a mathematically coherent review and derivation of influence functions for stationary points and perturbations to composite loss terms.
The qualitative influence heatmaps (e.g., Figures 2 and 3) offer an intuitive visual inspection of how spatial collocation points affect test-domain predictions.
weaknesses: The submission appears to be a 4-page workshop manuscript rather than a complete conference paper, containing unfinished sentences/placeholders (e.g., empty code availability statements on pages 1 and 5) and lacking the depth expected for the ICML main track.

The proposed Directional Indicator (DI) and Region Indicator (RI) are highly heuristic and task-specific to 2D unidirectional cylinder flow, lacking a principled framework that generalizes naturally to other PDEs or boundary configurations.

The empirical evaluation is restricted to a single 2D steady Navier-Stokes problem comparing only three hand-crafted model variants (good, bad, broken), without statistical error bars or validation across different PDE families.

There is no empirical validation comparing the influence function approximations against actual leave-one-out or leave-region-out retraining. Given known failure modes of Hessian-based influence functions in neural networks, verifying linear approximation accuracy in the PINN setting is crucial.

Scalability and computational cost are not critically evaluated; the experiments rely on `NaiveInfluenceFunction` on a tiny MLP (4 layers, 64 units), leaving open whether the approach is viable for modern, larger-scale scientific machine learning architectures.

strengths: Exploring training data attribution via influence functions (IFs) in the context of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) is a promising and conceptually well-motivated direction for interpretability and debugging in scientific machine learning.

The appendix provides an extensive and clean theoretical exposition extending influence function formulations to composite objective structures, loss weighting perturbations, and PDE parameter sensitivities.
The qualitative attribution heatmaps (Figures 2, 3, and 6) offer intuitive visualizations regarding how boundary conditions and obstacle geometry affect point predictions across the domain.
weaknesses: The manuscript is structured as a 4-page extended abstract or workshop paper rather than a complete, rigorous conference submission, lacking the depth, empirical scope, and comprehensive analysis expected for ICML.

No empirical validation is provided to verify whether the linear influence function approximation reliably tracks actual retraining counterfactuals (e.g., leave-one-out or group-removal retraining). Given well-documented issues with the fidelity and fragility of influence functions in deep non-convex architectures, ground-truth retraining validation is essential.

The experimental evaluation is restricted to a single toy setup (2D steady laminar Navier-Stokes flow around a cylinder) tested on only three model checkpoints ('good', 'broken', and 'bad'). The paper does not demonstrate generality across other PDE families (e.g., transient, hyperbolic, or higher-dimensional systems).

The proposed heuristic indicators do not convincingly separate the models in Table 1. For example, the under-sampled 'bad' model matches or exceeds the 'good' model on the Directional Indicator for $u_1$ (0.80 vs. 0.80) and pressure $p$ (0.87 vs. 0.83), weakening the claim that these metrics reliably diagnose physical fidelity.
There are no baseline comparisons against alternative data attribution or sensitivity techniques (e.g., TracIn, Fisher-based attributions, or simple leave-cluster-out retraining).

Several presentation and completeness flaws exist, including missing URLs where code availability was promised (both in the abstract and Section 'Code Availability'), as well as imprecise mathematical notation such as comparing 2D coordinate vectors directly via $x_{\text{train}} > x_{\text{test}}$ in Equation (5).

strengths: Novel and timely application: The paper introduces training data attribution to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), a domain where interpretability tools have been largely lacking despite the known verification challenges of PINNs (e.g., low training residuals not guaranteeing correct solutions).

Rigorous theoretical adaptation: The authors properly generalize classical influence functions to non-degenerate stationary points (saddle points) and composite multi-task objectives with arbitrary differentiable targets, proving bilinear decomposition and additivity across loss components and domain regions.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The framework is benchmarked across five time-dependent PDEs (Heat, Allen-Cahn, Burgers', Drift-Diffusion, Wave) and two steady-state PDEs (Poisson, Navier-Stokes), tested over 10 random seeds with statistical significance reported throughout.

Insightful diagnostic findings: The analysis reveals concrete, counter-intuitive structural characteristics, such as the fact that well-trained models display diminishing initial condition (IC) dependence and temporally balanced global influence, whereas persistent or heavily past-skewed influence is a hallmark of training failure.

Thorough methodological validation and transparency: The appendix provides extensive and necessary validation of the underlying approximations, including exact dense Hessian spectra, low-rank Arnoldi inverse-Hessian vector product (IHVP) fidelity via gradient cosine similarity, PBRF local fine-tuning correlation vs. raw leave-one-out retraining, continuous training data sweeps, and evaluations across multiple optimizers (Adam+L-BFGS, SOAP, NNCG).
weaknesses: Diagnostic only without active closed-loop intervention: While the paper outlines promising future directions for adaptive collocation resampling and loss reweighting in Appendix A.5, the work currently remains entirely post-hoc and does not evaluate whether influence-guided interventions actually outperform existing PINN sampling/reweighting schemes in practice.

Sensitivity to optimization paths and landscape geometry: As demonstrated in Appendix C.4, training with SOAP produces accurate solutions that nonetheless exhibit depressed indicator scores, showing that PINNFLUENCE reflects the specific stationary point reached rather than acting as an optimizer-invariant indicator of physical accuracy.

High cancellation in complex systems: Aggregating absolute influence magnitudes requires monitoring cancellation scores $\kappa$. In more complex coupled systems like the Navier-Stokes equations, high cancellation between conflicting constraints complicates the clean interpretability of fractional loss contributions.

Computational scalability: Although faster than full retraining and linear in sample sizes via Arnoldi caching, computing IHVPs across dense collocation and test sets remains computationally demanding, limiting the current demonstration to relatively small MLP architectures (3–5 layers, 32–100 hidden units).

strengths: Novel and timely bridge between training data attribution (TDA) and physics-informed machine learning, providing fine-grained interpretability for PINNs beyond simple residual inspection.

Sound theoretical grounding: carefully extends influence functions to non-degenerate stationary points and composite objectives, establishing linearity and additivity properties that enable rigorous decomposition across individual physics constraints (PDE residuals, initial conditions, boundary conditions).

Thorough empirical validation of the underlying approximations: the authors directly confront the known fragilities of influence functions in deep learning by evaluating Hessian spectra, validating low-rank Arnoldi projections via gradient cosine similarity, and validating influence predictions against Proximal Bregman Response Function (PBRF) fine-tuning across multiple PDEs.

Compelling diagnostic findings: demonstrates consistent structural markers across diverse benchmark PDEs (e.g., well-trained PINNs exhibit asymptotically diminishing IC influence and near-symmetric temporal influence, whereas poorly-trained models exhibit persistent IC over-reliance and skewed temporal attributions).

Extensive experimental evaluation and ablation studies: includes five time-dependent and two steady-state PDEs, multiple random seeds with error margins, continuous data sweeps, and validation across different optimizers (Adam+L-BFGS, SOAP, NNCG).
weaknesses: Diagnostic scope without empirical closed-loop intervention: although the manuscript outlines potential avenues for influence-guided resampling and loss reweighting (Appendix A.5), it does not experimentally validate whether closed-loop interventions based on PINNFLUENCE outperform established adaptive sampling (e.g., RAR, PINNACLE) or loss balancing schemes.

Computational scalability: while low-rank Arnoldi iteration and IHVP caching make the approach practical for the evaluated 1D and 2D benchmarks, evaluating full train-to-test pairwise influence matrices ($O((n+m)pk + nmk)$) remains computationally demanding for large-scale 3D spatio-temporal domains or large collocation sets.

PDE-dependent indicator sensitivity: as shown in the data-sweep and alternative optimizer experiments (e.g., the Wave equation and SOAP optimizer), regional and temporal indicators do not always behave monotonically or consistently across different equations, requiring practitioner domain knowledge to design and interpret appropriate indicators.

strengths: Novel and timely contribution: Adapting training data attribution via influence functions to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) fills a notable gap in scientific machine learning, where interpretability and post-hoc diagnostics are typically underdeveloped compared to training-dynamics analyses.

Sound theoretical formulation: The extension of influence functions to composite multi-objective losses, arbitrary differentiable output quantities f, and non-degenerate stationary points (Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 2.3) is mathematically rigorous and well-suited to the non-convex optimization landscapes of PINNs.

Comprehensive and well-designed diagnostic toolbox: The framework provides practical diagnostic primitives, including point-to-region attributions, loss-component decompositions, cancellation scores, and temporal/directional indicators that reveal structural properties invisible to standard residual inspection.

Extensive empirical validation and sanity checks: The method is validated across seven PDE benchmarks (five time-dependent and two steady-state) with multiple random seeds. The authors thoroughly address common pitfalls of influence functions in Appendix A and C, including low-rank Arnoldi inverse-Hessian validation against true gradients, PBRF vs. LOO correlation analysis, computational complexity benchmarks, and evaluation across different optimizers (e.g., SOAP, NNCG).

Insightful empirical discoveries: The paper uncovers counterintuitive structural insights, such as demonstrating that well-trained PINNs exhibit near-symmetric temporal influence rather than causally oriented influence, whereas strong early-time/IC dominance is a characteristic signature of optimization failure.
weaknesses: Lack of closed-loop active intervention experiments: While the authors outline promising applications of PINNFLUENCE for adaptive collocation resampling and dynamic loss re-weighting (Appendix A.5), the paper remains purely diagnostic. Demonstrating an end-to-end active training intervention guided by influence scores would have substantially bolstered the practical significance.

Inherent fragility of influence approximations: Consistent with known literature on deep networks, influence estimates show virtually zero correlation with true leave-one-out retraining from scratch (Table 5). While correlation with local fine-tuning (PBRF) is documented, Spearman rank correlations remain relatively modest for several configurations (e.g., poorly-trained Drift-Diffusion at 0.08, Wave at 0.15).

Domain-specific indicator engineering: Beyond generic pointwise influence and loss decompositions, designing meaningful regional and directional indicators requires manual specification and prior knowledge of the PDE's underlying geometry and physical behavior, which limits fully automated diagnostic pipelines.
